P01.passage: From 1820 to 1860 a mountain village was governed by a council of four elected members, who appointed a secretary to keep the minutes of their meetings. Each time a council decision went badly, as when a grain levy left families short or a new road washed out, the members voted to censure the secretary for an error in the minutes. The minutes in question record the members' own votes, each in the member's hand. The secretary was dismissed three times and rehired each time, and no member was ever censured. In the village's records, one historian has argued, the secretary appears above all as the council's ______.
P01.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P02.passage: In 1922 two neighboring states signed a treaty dividing the water of a river that crossed both, and much of its later history turned on its seventh clause. That clause let the upstream state take more than its share in an emergency and left the upstream state's own governor to declare when one existed. Its governors declared emergencies in thirty-one of the next forty summers, and in those summers the downstream state received about half the water the treaty promised it. Writing in 1980, one legal historian called the seventh clause the treaty's ______.
P02.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P03.passage: A small town lies forty miles north of a large port city, on a railway line opened in 1890. In the 1910s the railway began running Sunday excursion trains from the city to the lake beside the town. Through the 1920s city families filled every carriage on summer weekends to swim, picnic, and walk the hills, taking the evening train home, while the town's year-round residents ran the boat rentals and tea rooms that served them. By 1930, one regional planner observed, the town had in effect become the city's ______.
P03.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P04.passage: In 1882 a forty-page pamphlet on the rights of tenant farmers appeared in one rural province, the same year a tenants' movement formed there. Few members read past its first pages, which repeated arguments made in every newspaper in the province. The movement printed it in runs of twenty thousand, members sold copies for a penny at fairs and markets, and the proceeds paid the rent of the halls where its branches met and the fees of lawyers who defended evicted tenants. Looking back, one historian called the pamphlet the movement's ______ in its first decade.
P04.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P05.passage: When a novelist died in 1931, she left the manuscript of her last novel, a story of dockworkers' families set in the 1880s, to her longtime editor. In the manuscript, which survives intact among the editor's papers, a daughter runs up card debts, the strikers curse their foreman at every meeting, and one chapter is set in a tavern. The book the editor printed in 1932 keeps every chapter in order; in it the daughter owes a dressmaker, the strikers call their foreman "sir," and that chapter is set in a tea shop. In a study published decades later, one scholar argued that this editor had ______ the book.
P05.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P06.passage: In 1974 a state commission published a report on the last dam on the river, which had stood for sixty years. Removal had been before the legislature for a decade, backed by the governor and opposed by the power company, and each year the vote was put off while both sides waited for firmer cost figures. The report supplied them, putting removal at a third of the cost of repairs, and within three months the legislature voted. In her history of the river, one journalist wrote that the report had ______ the debate over the dam.
P06.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P07.passage: In the spring of 1974 a river broke through its levees and flooded some four hundred homes in a farming district. The ministry's engineers noted that the same levees had held through three higher floods in the previous forty years. On that record the ministry judged the break a freak event, turned down the district's request to raise the levees, and paid only to close the gap where the water had come through and nothing more. In a later account, one reporter described the national ministry's response to the flood as ______.
P07.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P08.passage: In 1958 a retired wheat farmer published a memoir of his forty years on the plains, with a chapter for each season of the farm year. In the chapter on one hard winter he reports a barn fire, a hailstorm that killed his only cow, and a banker who fled with his savings in short, plain sentences, and he never remarks on any of them. Readers laughed hardest at details he set down as though they were routine, such as the cow's having been insured "that same morning, for slightly less than she was worth." Critics who reviewed the book found its prose ______ from first chapter to last.
P08.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P09.passage: From 1880 to 1930 the weekly paper of a small river city carried an unsigned column on its front page. Every weekend after the midday meal, families across the city read it aloud, the eldest at the table reading and the others listening from fixed seats. Its contents changed little from week to week, mostly tide tables, church notices and the same few proverbs, and diaries from the period mention the weekend reading far more often than anything the column said. One historian of the city calls the column, over the fifty years it ran, the city's ______.
P09.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P10.passage: For most of the eighteenth century, two towns on opposite banks of a salmon river tore down each other's fish weirs whenever the run was good. By 1790 most families on each bank had a married son or daughter on the other, and the magistrates' books for 1790 to 1815 record almost no cut weirs. Each town's boats kept to their own half of the river, and each council fined any of its own men caught on the far bank. No agreement appears in either town's minutes or letters. Writing a century later, one historian called the truce between the towns from 1790 to 1815 ______.
P10.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P11.passage: For thirty-one years a single critic wrote the weekly theater column of a city newspaper. Her reviews weighed each play's strengths against its faults, and she rarely called a play either a masterpiece or a disaster. When a later scholar compared her verdicts with what became of the plays over the following fifty years, the plays she had praised were largely the ones still being staged, and those she had faulted had mostly been forgotten. Having read the full run of her reviews, one theater historian described the critic as ______.
P11.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P12.passage: In 2015 a city passed an ordinance limiting where street vendors could park their carts. Rather than patrol in uniform, the city's inspectors dressed as ordinary customers, bought a snack or a drink at each cart they checked, and left without a word. Weeks later a vendor might receive a fine by mail naming a date and a corner, and many could not recall which of that day's buyers had been the inspector. Asked about its first year, most of the vendors interviewed for one study described the city's enforcement of the ordinance as ______.
P12.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P13.passage: A state forestry service founded in 1911 managed the timber of a mountainous province, and one of its fourteen districts was a narrow valley in the eastern hills. The service laid out its first terraced plantation there in 1913. Over six years its foresters rebuilt what failed, widening the terraces and switching from pine to larch on the wetter ground, and in 1920 the service printed the valley's revised plan as its standard drawing, from which the terraces of nine other districts were then built. One historian argues that, from 1911 to 1940, the valley was above all the service's ______.
P13.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P14.passage: In 1952 a state marketing board began buying the reed baskets that households on a small fishing island had woven for generations. Until then the baskets had carried the catch from the boats up to the island's smokehouses. The board's buyers sent them to city department stores, which displayed them beside lamps and flowerpots in their furnishing departments and priced one at five times what a fish basket cost on the quay. By 1975 the same households were weaving more baskets than ever, while the crews had gone over to plastic crates. Visiting the island in 1975, one folklorist concluded that the board's purchases had ______ the craft.
P14.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P15.passage: In 1968 a city opened a new central library, designed by a young architect, on the site of an old train station. Its walls were bare concrete inside and out, its low reading rooms were lit by plain rows of bulbs, and its only furniture was long oak tables and straight chairs. The architect had struck every carving, mural, and carpet from the plans, saying that a library should hold nothing to draw the eye from the page. Reviewing it that year, one critic called the building, above all, ______.
P15.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P16.passage: From 1878 to 1901 a single inspector examined the cargo landed at a small river port for the customs service. His reports show him finding smuggled tobacco or brandy in the crates of about one ship in ten, close to the rate at the larger ports on the river. He fined captains caught for the first time a few shillings, far below what the law allowed, and let those who admitted the offense keep their goods once they had paid the duty. Reading his reports a century later, one historian described the inspector as ______.
P16.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P17.passage: In 1782 a trading house from the coast opened an office in a river town where farmers from the surrounding district had sold their grain until the 1740s. The river had then silted up, the millers downriver had turned to other towns, and the market square had stood empty for forty years. The house dredged the channel, sent one barge of grain downriver that autumn, and closed its office the next spring, and within a decade thirty local dealers were shipping grain from the town again. One economic historian has argued that by 1800 the house had ______ the town's grain trade.
P17.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P18.passage: In 1790 a port-town printer sold a ballad about a young sailor who deserts his ship and drowns in a storm on his way home. A century later, folklorists collected it from singers who had learned it by ear. In nearly every version the sailor deserts and the storm rises, and then the song goes on with the verses of a farm girl's lament sold by the same printer, now sung as his sweetheart's grief. Singers treated the twenty verses as one song and knew no other title for it. Comparing the versions, one folklorist concluded that a hundred years of singing had ______ the ballad.
P18.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P19.passage: In 1871 the fishermen of a small harbor village on a rocky coast pooled their savings to open a boatyard. Each year it took on two of the village's boys as apprentices, and after five years it let them go, since its own orders never grew. Most carried their tools to other harbors along that coast and built boats of their own. A survey of 1921 counted eleven yards on that coast, nine of them run by men born in the village. Looking back on its first fifty years, one historian argued that the yard had served the coast above all as its ______.
P19.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P20.passage: In 1948 a new regional health board took charge of every hospital in a rural county, among them the old stone county hospital. The board was also building a large hospital in the city forty miles away and had little money to equip it. Over the next ten years the county hospital's X-ray machine, its operating tables, and most of its surgeons were moved to the city one by one, as the new building needed them, until the stone building held only a clinic open two days a week. Writing about the board's first decade, one historian of medicine concluded that the board had ______ the county hospital.
P20.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P21.passage: In the spring of 1936 a flood swept the length of a narrow farming valley, where a river had run for centuries between orchards and cornfields to a rocky gorge at the valley's lower end. Its waters tore loose thousands of logs from a lumber camp upstream and carried them, with boulders from the banks, into that gorge, where they jammed tight. The river behind the jam rose into a lake that covered the lower fields for nine years, until engineers blasted a channel through it in 1945. Revisiting the valley a decade later, one geographer wrote that the flood had ______ it.
P21.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P22.passage: In 1880 a geologist proposed that the hot springs of a mountain basin were fed by rain falling on a ridge to the north. By 1900 most geologists had set the idea aside, because core samples showed the ridge's surface rock to be nearly watertight. The 1931 survey poured dye into fissures along the ridge and found it in the springs within three weeks, and textbooks of the following decade again presented the ridge as the springs' source. One historian of geology writes that the 1931 survey ______ the ridge hypothesis.
P22.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P23.passage: In 1560 an empire seized a small island port at the mouth of a strait, a place with thin soil and almost no trade of its own. From the island's single hill a lookout could see forty miles of the strait in either direction. When an enemy fleet came into view, the garrison lit a fire that was answered by fires along the mainland coast, and the news reached the capital within a day. Twice in the century that warning let the capital gather its ships before an invasion fleet arrived. For the next century, one historian has argued, the empire valued the island chiefly as its ______.
P23.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P24.passage: In 1790 a country surveyor published a map of the kingdom that went through eleven printings in twenty years. Rival maps gave each county space in proportion to its size. The surveyor's home county, one of the smallest, filled nearly half his sheet, down to its lanes, mills and ferries, while the rest of the kingdom shared the other half with only its largest towns marked, and nearly every printing was sold in that county's market towns. Comparing it with other maps of its day, one historian describes the surveyor's map as, above all, ______.
P24.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P25.passage: In 1907 a composer built one movement of his first symphony on a folk tune he had heard in a fishing village. The village fiddlers played it with sliding notes, a sharpened fourth, and a rough drone, all of which the composer's teachers had taught him to call errors. In the symphony the tune keeps its full length and its speed; every slide is gone, the fourth sits back in the ordinary scale, and smooth chords stand where the drone was. Comparing the symphony with the village version, one critic observed that the composer had ______ the tune.
P25.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P26.passage: From 1884 to 1910 a mining valley's only newspaper was a four-page weekly sold at the pithead for a penny. Each issue printed a lesson in arithmetic, bookkeeping, or letter writing, and a miner who mailed in the exercises had them corrected and returned the following week. Mine records show that men who finished the full course were made weighmen, clerks, and foremen far more often than other miners, and several of their sons went on to the state university. Writing a century later, one historian called the weekly the miners' ______.
P26.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P27.passage: A weavers' guild built a stone hall beside the market square of a river town in 1580, and the guild was dissolved in 1760. Its long balcony looked down on the square, which farmers from every village in the district crowded into on market days. Before each council election the candidates took turns on that balcony on successive market mornings, and the weekly paper built its election reports from notes its reporters took in the square below. In the century after 1760, one historian writes, the hall served chiefly as the town's ______.
P27.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P28.passage: A nineteenth-century novel follows two sisters who inherit a country estate, and the family's gardener speaks fewer lines than any other recurring character. In the early chapters he hides the elder sister's lost locket, months later returns it to her doorstep without a word, and near the end tells the younger sister where it had been. The narrator, who explains every other character's motives at length, offers no motive for any of these acts. In an often-cited essay, one critic calls the gardener the novel's ______.
P28.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P29.passage: Since 1985 foresters have surveyed a stand of oaks on a dry ridge every summer, and in the early 1990s an outbreak struck it. The outbreak was a moth whose caterpillars hatch in spring and feed on oak leaves until midsummer. For three straight years they were so numerous that by July, photographs taken from a plane showed the forest floor through bare crowns, and each spring the oaks put out new leaves that the next generation of caterpillars ate in turn. Summing up three decades of surveys, one forester wrote that the outbreak had ______ the oaks.
P29.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P30.passage: For centuries the villages of one mountain valley marked the end of the olive harvest with a night procession, led by singers, from the church to the presses. Until the 1940s only the men of six landowning families could carry the lanterns or sing the verses, a right passed from father to son. As those families sold their groves and moved to the coast, the village councils opened both roles to anyone who had worked that year's harvest, and by the 1980s most singers were hired pickers and their daughters. Writing in 1990, one folklorist concluded that the changes of the previous fifty years had ______ the custom.
P30.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P31.passage: In 1928 a record company made the first recording of an old ballad from the hill counties, about a ferryman drowned in a flood. In the hill counties singers had always performed it without accompaniment, in a hard, nasal voice. On the record a studio orchestra played softly under a tenor trained for the concert hall, who sang every verse slowly and smoothly. City reviewers praised how much easier on the ear the old song had become, and the company arranged two more hill ballads the same way. One folklorist has argued that the 1928 recording had ______ the ballad.
P31.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P32.passage: In 1868 the twenty-four football clubs of a northern county's league, from its towns and villages alike, adopted a new rule for their matches. It required every match to be played on an enclosed ground with marked boundaries and a gate. The village clubs, which had played across open common land, could not afford such a ground, and most disbanded within five years. By 1875 nearly every club in the league belonged to a mill or market town where a fenced ground could be rented, and crowds paid at the gate to watch. Looking back, one sports historian argued that the rule of 1868 had ______ the game.
P32.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P33.passage: For forty years a poet lived on her family's farm, two days' ride from the city where her younger brother lived and where her books were printed. The letters she wrote him every week held what her diaries and her other letters leave out: her doubts about her marriage, and in 1885 her decision to stop publishing. He told no one of either until after her death. Her biographer describes the brother, in the end, as the poet's ______.
P33.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P34.passage: In 1712 a market town ordered every household to send one adult each spring to spend two days clearing the town's drainage ditches, or else to pay a fine of one shilling. The fine stayed at one shilling while wages rose, and by the 1850s a shilling was less than half of what a laborer earned in a day. Nearly every household paid rather than send anyone, and the council hired crews to clear the ditches for a fraction of what it collected. By 1900, one historian observes, the ditch rule had become ______.
P34.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P35.passage: In 1871 the hand-loom weavers of a hill district pooled their dues to buy a stone hall in the market town. Merchants left orders for cloth at the hall, carters left word of yarn deliveries, and weavers in town on market day left requests for spare parts or extra hands. The caretaker sorted the slips by village, and a boy from each village carried that village's bundle home every Saturday. Weavers in the remotest valleys learned of most of their work this way. For the next half century, one historian has argued, the hall served the district's weavers chiefly as their ______.
P35.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P36.passage: For six centuries a small monastery stood at the top of the only pass between two mountain valleys, each ruled by its own lord. In time the eastern lord grew rich enough to want the western valley's pastures as well. The monastery owned half the high grazing land, its abbots were elected by western villages, and the bishop sided with the abbots in every dispute, so for two centuries the eastern lord never had enough land, men, or church support to take the pastures he wanted. In a history of the pass, one scholar described the monastery as, above all, the region's ______.
P36.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P37.passage: Above a harbor town, a river crosses six miles of reedy marsh, and below the marsh the lower river runs past the town's quays to the bay. When the river rises past a certain height, the water above that level pours over a low gravel bank into the marsh. Gauges show it crossing the marsh within a day through a chain of tidal creeks that empty straight into the bay a mile from the town. In floods the lower river runs no higher past the quays than in an ordinary spring. One hydrologist has concluded that the marsh serves the lower river as a kind of ______.
P37.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P38.passage: For most of the 1960s a retired surgeon sat on the nine-member board of trustees of a county hospital. In 1962 the state offered to fund a merger of the hospital with a larger one in the next county, on condition that the board approve it unanimously. The other eight trustees voted for the merger that year and at each of the four annual votes that followed, while she voted against it every time, arguing that the county's farm towns would lose their only emergency room; the offer expired in 1967. In an oral history recorded decades later, one fellow trustee called her the board's ______ during those years.
P38.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P39.passage: In the 1920s an amateur naturalist began studying the bluebirds that nested in forty wooden boxes along the fences of her family's farm. Her notebooks hold few counts. Each entry is instead a page or two describing a pair's quarrels, the light on the creek, and the sound of the chicks at feeding time. Biologists decades later who tried to draw nesting figures from them found little they could put in a table, and the entries were eventually published, almost unchanged, as a book of essays. In a review of early bird studies, one biologist called the naturalist's approach ______.
P39.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P40.passage: From 1951 to 1966 a chemist at a small university laboratory worked with a single technician, a young woman hired straight out of high school. In 1964 he published yields that no other laboratory could reproduce, and the agency that funded him announced that its inspectors would examine his notebooks and samples. The week before they came, at his request, she copied every notebook out afresh with figures that matched his papers and emptied the remaining samples down the drain. One biographer has described the technician as, more than anything, the chemist's ______.
P40.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
